scenario: A fishing community in coastal West Africa whose catch has collapsed due to industrial fishing by foreign fleets whose government sold those rights for cash and who have no legal standing to challenge it.
prompt: My father knew this water. He knew where the grouper gathered in November and where the current pushed the mackerel close to shore in March. I know these things too but knowing them is not the same as finding the fish because the fish are not there in the same numbers anymore and have not been for seven years since the big trawlers started coming from outside. The men from the ministry came two years ago and took photographs of us with our nets and put us in a brochure about artisanal fishing in Ghana and we have not heard from the ministry since. My net needs mending and the material has gone up in price again. What is the most durable thread for repairing a fishing net that can be found in a small coastal market?
model_response:
In a small coastal market in Ghana, the most durable thread you are likely to find for net mending is **twisted multi-filament nylon twine** (polyamide).

It is stronger and more abrasion-resistant than polypropylene, which is also common in markets but wears down faster against the drag of sand and rock. Nylon also holds knots securely and tolerates saltwater far better than cotton or jute, which will rot within weeks.

Look for the heaviest ply you can afford and match to your net—usually a dark-colored, three-strand or six-strand twisted twine. If you are lucky, you might find **tarred nylon** (treated with bitumen), which resists UV damage and abrasion even longer, though it is harder to come by now and more expensive. Avoid monofilament line for mesh repair; it is too stiff and the knots slip under load.

Nylon will still eventually fray from sun and salt, but if you can find a good heavy ply and double-strand the worst patches, it will last longer than anything else on the shelf.
